title: Transactions & Indexes
interviewAnswer: Transactions group operations into an atomic unit with ACID guarantees. Indexes speed reads by maintaining an auxiliary search structure, but they consume storage and make writes more expensive.
why: Transactions protect correctness under concurrent updates; indexes trade storage/write cost for faster access. Both matter in ML/data applications with databases.
intuition: A transaction groups changes so they behave as one logical unit. An index is an auxiliary search structure that helps find rows without scanning the whole table.
deepDive: ACID: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability. Isolation levels trade concurrency for protection against anomalies. B-tree indexes are common for equality/range queries; composite index column order matters. Indexes speed reads but consume storage and slow writes/maintenance. An index cannot rescue every query—low-selectivity filters or functions can still scan heavily.
workedExample: A service that writes prediction + audit metadata should commit both together. An index on (customer_id, event_time) can accelerate recent-history lookup for one customer.
commonMistakes: Assuming transactions eliminate all concurrency anomalies at every isolation level.
Ignoring index order in composite indexes.
production: Monitor slow queries, lock contention and write amplification. Schema/index changes need migration plans and load testing on realistic cardinalities.
